flashcards.q: State the precise definition of a p-value.
flashcards.a: P(data this extreme or more extreme | H0 is true) -- the probability of observing a test statistic at least this extreme, ASSUMING the null hypothesis holds. It is NOT P(H0 true | data), and going from one to the other requires Bayes' theorem plus a prior on H0, which a p-value alone doesn't provide.

flashcards.q: Define Type I and Type II error and the tradeoff between them.
flashcards.a: Type I (alpha): rejecting a TRUE null -- false positive; you set this directly, usually 0.05. Type II (beta): failing to reject a FALSE null -- false negative; power = 1-beta. Holding sample size fixed, lowering alpha increases beta (fewer false positives but more missed real effects). Only increasing sample size reduces both.

flashcards.q: Give the approximate sample size per group needed to detect small/medium/large effect sizes at alpha=0.05, power=0.80.
flashcards.a: Small effect (Cohen's d=0.2): ~393 per group. Medium (d=0.5): ~64 per group. Large (d=0.8): ~26 per group. Sample size requirements grow sharply as the true effect shrinks -- this is why realistic small product-experiment effects need large samples.

flashcards.q: What does a significant one-way ANOVA tell you, and what doesn't it tell you?
flashcards.a: It tells you at least one group's mean differs from at least one other's (the omnibus F-test rejects 'all means equal'). It does NOT tell you which group(s) differ, by how much, or in which direction -- that requires a post-hoc test like Tukey's HSD.

flashcards.q: Why can't you just run pairwise t-tests on every pair of groups after a significant ANOVA?
flashcards.a: It reintroduces the multiple-comparisons problem the ANOVA omnibus test was meant to control for. With 3 groups, 3 pairwise t-tests at alpha=0.05 each gives a family-wise error rate of 1-0.95^3 ~= 14.3%, not 5%. Use Tukey's HSD instead, which corrects for the number of pairwise comparisons.

flashcards.q: What is the actual family-wise false-positive rate from running 5 independent tests at alpha=0.05 each with no correction? And 20 tests?
flashcards.a: 1-(1-0.05)^k. At k=5: 1-0.95^5 ~= 22.6%. At k=20: 1-0.95^20 ~= 64.2% -- you're more likely than not to see at least one spurious 'significant' result.

flashcards.q: Bonferroni vs Benjamini-Hochberg (fdr_bh) correction -- what does each control and which is more conservative?
flashcards.a: Bonferroni divides alpha by k, controlling the family-wise error rate (probability of ANY false positive) -- simple but conservative, loses power fast as k grows. Benjamini-Hochberg controls the false discovery rate (expected proportion of false positives AMONG rejections) -- less conservative, standard when testing many hypotheses at scale.

flashcards.q: What is 'peeking' in A/B testing and why does it break your statistics?
flashcards.a: Checking a running experiment's significance repeatedly and stopping the moment it crosses threshold, rather than waiting for a pre-planned sample size. Each peek is effectively another implicit hypothesis test, and stopping at the first 'significant' peek inflates the TRUE Type I error rate far above the nominal alpha -- the multiple-comparisons problem in disguise.

flashcards.q: How do you fix the peeking problem in A/B testing?
flashcards.a: Either fix the sample size via a power analysis before starting and don't interpret significance before reaching it, or use a sequential testing method (group sequential design, or always-valid/mSPRT-based inference) explicitly designed to control Type I error under continuous monitoring.

flashcards.q: What is sample ratio mismatch (SRM) and why does it invalidate an A/B test regardless of the treatment-effect p-value?
flashcards.a: The observed traffic split doesn't match the intended split (configured 50/50, observed 54/46). It signals a broken randomization/logging/bot-filtering pipeline, and whatever mechanism skewed the ratio may also have skewed group COMPOSITION, confounding any treatment effect estimate regardless of what its own p-value says.

flashcards.q: Explain Simpson's paradox in an A/B testing context.
flashcards.a: An aggregate metric shows variant B losing overall, while B actually wins within every individual segment (new users, returning users, etc). This happens when segment composition is unbalanced between arms -- e.g. treatment got proportionally more of a low-converting segment -- confounding the aggregate comparison even though every within-segment comparison is clean.

flashcards.q: When should you use Fisher's exact test instead of chi-square test of independence?
flashcards.a: When expected cell counts are small (common rule of thumb: expected count >= 5 in at least 80% of cells). Chi-square relies on a large-sample approximation to the chi-square distribution that becomes unreliable with sparse contingency tables; Fisher's exact test computes exact probabilities without that approximation.

flashcards.q: Why is Welch's t-test often the safer default over Student's t-test?
flashcards.a: Student's t-test assumes equal variance between groups, which real-world groups rarely have exactly. Welch's t-test doesn't assume equal variance and degrades gracefully to essentially the same answer as Student's when variances ARE equal, at negligible cost -- so it's a safer default in practice (scipy: ttest_ind(equal_var=False)).

flashcards.q: Does a non-significant result (p > 0.05) prove there's no effect?
flashcards.a: No. It could mean the test was underpowered for the true effect size -- 'not significant' means 'we didn't have enough evidence to detect it,' which is different from 'evidence of no effect.' Report power and effect-size confidence intervals alongside a non-significant p-value, not the p-value alone.
